### Three moves are sufficient

Move blocks \(A,B,C\) as follows:

- Turn \(A\) horizontally across the top-left.
- Move \(B\) horizontally to the second row on the left.
- Turn \(C\) vertically in column \(4\).

The new arrangement is

```text
A A A C E
B B B C E
· D · C E
· D F F F
· D G G G
```

Only \(A,B,C\) have moved. The three squares in column \(1\), rows \(3\) through \(5\), are now empty, so another \(1\times3\) block fits there.

### Why two moves cannot suffice

Let \(x=(3,3)\), \(p=(4,1)\), \(q=(5,1)\), and \(r=(3,4)\). Initially the empty squares are \(x,p,q,r\).

Color each square \((i,j)\) by \(i+j\pmod 3\), and again by \(i-j\pmod 3\). Every \(1\times3\) block, whether horizontal or vertical, covers one square of each color in both colorings. Therefore the color counts of the empty squares never change.

For both colorings, the initial empty squares have colors \(0,0,1,2\). A straight \(1\times3\) empty strip has one square of each color, so its fourth accompanying empty square must have color \(0\) in both colorings. Hence

\[
i+j\equiv0,\qquad i-j\equiv0\pmod3,
\]

which forces \(i=j=3\). Thus \(x=(3,3)\) must remain the extra empty square, and the new straight gap cannot pass through it.

Checking how many of \(p,q,r\) can lie in the new strip:

- All three cannot lie in one straight strip.
- If two lie in it, they must be \(p,q\), giving the vertical strip in column \(1\), rows \(3\)–\(5\). Vacating its square \((3,1)\) requires moving \(A\), while filling \(r\) requires moving two more blocks to supply the vertical strip through \(r\).
- If exactly one lies in it, the corresponding moved blocks and the blocks needed to refill the other empty squares again require at least three moved blocks.
- If none lies in it, filling \(p,q,r\) requires at least three moved blocks.

Therefore two moves are impossible, while the construction above shows that three moves suffice.
